claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: SMG, pMTG, and PMd have shown some of the greatest evolutionary expansion in humans.
claims.source: the supramarginal gyrus (SMG), posterior middle temporal gyrus (pMTG), and dorsal premotor cortex (PMd)—areas that have shown some of the greatest evolutionary expansion in humans (Van Essen and Dierker, 2007)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Human occipitotemporal cortex contains body-selective regions for perception, such as the extrastriate body area (EBA).
claims.source: fMRI studies further suggest that human occipitotemporal cortex also contains body-selective regions for perception, such as the extrastriate body area (EBA), which preferentially respond to viewing of the body and its parts (Astafiev et al., 2004; David et al., 2007; Peelen and Downing, 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous fMRI research.

claims.claim: The frontoparietal regions activated by tools are spatially close to brain areas implicated in hand actions, particularly the grip component of reach-to-grasp actions.
claims.source: The frontoparietal regions activated by tools are spatially close to (and perhaps overlapping with) brain areas implicated in hand actions, particularly the grip component of reach-to-grasp actions.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the spatial organization of brain regions.

claims.claim: SMG lies very near the grasp-selective anterior intraparietal sulcus (aIPS).
claims.source: Specifically, SMG lies very near the grasp-selective anterior intraparietal sulcus (aIPS, Chao and Martin, 2000; Valyear et al., 2007)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: PMd shows grasp-selective as well as tool-selective responses.
claims.source: and PMd shows grasp-selective as well as tool-selective responses (Grezes and Decety, 2002; Gallivan et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Real hand actions activate frontoparietal regions including SPOC, PMd, and additional areas along the IPS.
claims.source: In addition, real hand actions activate other frontoparietal regions including the superior parieto-occipital cortex (SPOC) region, PMd, and additional areas along the IPS (Culham et al., 2006; Filimon, 2010)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Almost all human neuroimaging studies of tools to date have used proxies for real tool use.
claims.source: Moreover, almost all of the human neuroimaging studies of tools to date have used proxies for real tool use (reviewed in Lewis, 2006), including visual stimuli such as images or movies (e.g., Beauchamp et al., 2002), semantic tasks (e.g., Martin et al., 1995), or simulated tool actions like pantomiming, imitating or imagining tool use (e.g., Johnson-Frey et al., 2005; Rumiati et al., 2004) or making perceptual judgments about how one would use a tool (e.g., Jacobs et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and a review.

claims.claim: Thirteen right-handed subjects participated in the Motor experiment.
claims.source: fMRI (3 Tesla) was used to measure the blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) signal in the brains of 13 right-handed subjects (7 females; mean age: 25.7 years)
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods.

claims.claim: Subjects used either the right hand or a tool controlled by the right hand to execute movements.
claims.source: Subjects used either the right hand or a tool (controlled by the right hand) to execute a precision reach-to-grasp (Grasp) or reach-to-touch (Reach) movement towards a single centrally located real three-dimensional (3D) target object made of Lego blocks (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods, with reference to a figure.

claims.claim: The tool used was a set of reverse tongs that required different hand kinematics compared to when the hand was used alone.
claims.source: The tool used was a set of reverse tongs; when the hand closed on the grips, the ends of the tongs would open and vice versa. As such, different hand kinematics were required to operate the tool compared to when the hand was used alone.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods.

claims.claim: The position of the target object was changed between hand and tool experimental runs.
claims.source: The position of the target object was changed between hand and tool experimental runs in order for the grasps and reaches to be performed at a comfortable distance for each effector (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods, with reference to a figure.

claims.claim: The delay timing of the paradigm allowed isolation of sustained plan-related neural responses from visual and movement execution responses.
claims.source: The delay timing of the paradigm allowed us to divide the trial into discrete time epochs and isolate the sustained plan-related neural responses that evolve prior to movement from the transient visual response (Preview phase) and the movement execution response (Execute phase; Figure 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design and its purpose, with reference to figures.

claims.claim: MVPA was performed to decode preparatory signals and determine where movement plans for hand and tool were distinct versus shared.
claims.source: Using multi-voxel pattern analysis (MVPA) to decode preparatory (pre-movement) signals, we then probed exactly where in frontoparietal cortex and in tool- and body-selective areas in occipitotemporal cortex movement plans (grasping vs reaching) for the hand and tool were distinct (effector-specific) vs where signals related to upcoming actions of the hand could be used to predict the same actions performed with the tool (effector-independent).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the analytical methods used.

claims.claim: Preparatory signals in SPOC and EBA differentiated upcoming movements of the hand only.
claims.source: Consistent with an effector-specific coding of hand- and tool-related movements we found that preparatory signals in SPOC and EBA differentiated upcoming movements of the hand only (i.e., hand-specific)
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Preparatory signals in SMG and pMTG discriminated upcoming movements of the tool only.
claims.source: whereas in SMG and pMTG they discriminated upcoming movements of the tool only (i.e., tool-specific).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: In anterior parietal regions (e.g., aIPS) and motor cortex, pre-movement activity patterns discriminated planned actions of both the hand and tool but could not be used to predict upcoming actions of the other effector.
claims.source: In addition, in anterior parietal regions (e.g., aIPS) and motor cortex we found that pre-movement activity patterns discriminated planned actions of 'both' the hand and tool but, importantly, could not be used to predict upcoming actions of the other effector.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Effector-independent coding was constrained to preparatory signals of posterior IPS and premotor cortex.
claims.source: Instead, we found that this effector-independent type of coding was constrained to the preparatory signals of a subset of frontoparietal areas (posterior IPS and premotor cortex)
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: In posterior IPS and premotor cortex, neural representations are more tightly linked to the goal of the action rather than the specific hand movements required.
claims.source: suggesting that in these regions neural representations are more tightly linked to the goal of the action (grasping vs reaching) rather than the specific hand movements required to implement those goals.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Ten commonly described neuroanatomical ROIs in the left hemisphere were localized for MVPA analysis.
claims.source: Within this network, we focused MVPA on 10 commonly described neuroanatomical ROIs in the left hemisphere (contralateral to the arm used), each previously implicated in either hand-related and/or tool-related processing.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the analytical methods.

claims.claim: SPOC, pIPS, midIPS, motor cortex, and PMd are areas generally implicated in hand-related movement planning processes.
claims.source: We localized superior parieto-occipital cortex (SPOC), posterior intraparietal sulcus (pIPS), middle IPS (midIPS), motor cortex, and dorsal premotor (PMd) cortex—a group of well-known parietal and frontal areas generally implicated in hand-related movement planning processes in human and/or macaque cortex (Culham et al., 2006; Andersen and Cui, 2009; Cisek and Kalaska, 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: aIPS, post. aIPS, SMG, and PMv are areas generally implicated in hand preshaping and tool-related processes.
claims.source: In addition, we defined the anterior intraparietal sulcus (aIPS), a region just posterior to aIPS (post. aIPS), supramarginal gyrus (SMG), and ventral premotor (PMv) cortex—a group of parietal and frontal areas generally implicated in hand preshaping and tool-related processes (Rizzolatti and Luppino, 2001; Culham et al., 2006; Lewis, 2006; Umilta et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: SS-cortex was selected as a sensory control region not expected to accurately decode movements until stimulation of the hand's mechanoreceptors at movement onset.
claims.source: One additional area, left somatosensory (SS-cortex), was selected as a sensory control region, not expected to accurately decode movements until stimulation of the hand's mechanoreceptors at movement onset (i.e., at the Execute phase).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design and expectations.

claims.claim: Time-resolved decoding analysis revealed a full range of decoding profiles during movement planning across the network of specified regions.
claims.source: This time-resolved decoding analysis revealed a full range of decoding profiles during movement planning across the network of specified regions.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Preparatory voxel patterns in nearly all regions could be used to predict the action performed for both the hand and tool effector.
claims.source: Notably, in nearly all the remaining regions, we were able to successfully use the activity patterns to predict the action performed (grasping vs reaching) for both the hand and tool effector (Figures 3–5, red and blue decoding traces; purple traces will be discussed in the next section entitled 'Separate and shared representations for the hand and tool').
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results, with reference to figures.

claims.claim: In parietal cortex, preparatory activity in pIPS, midIPS, post. aIPS, aIPS, and t-aIPS could be used to accurately discriminate which object-directed hand or tool movement was to be performed.
claims.source: For instance, in parietal cortex, preparatory activity in pIPS, midIPS, post. aIPS, aIPS, and t-aIPS could be used to accurately discriminate which object-directed hand or tool movement was to be performed moments later
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: In frontal cortex, predictive movement activity for hand and tool actions was found in motor cortex, PMd, and PMv.
claims.source: Likewise, in frontal cortex, predictive movement activity for hand and tool actions was also found in motor cortex, PMd, and PMv.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: SS-cortex failed to decode any planned movements and only discriminated the different actions upon execution.
claims.source: Importantly, consistent with expectations and previous investigations (Gallivan et al., 2011a, 2011b), our sensory control region, SS-cortex, failed to decode any planned movements and only discriminated the different actions upon execution (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results, with reference to a figure and citations.

claims.claim: Accurate across-effector classification was found in four regions during planning: pIPS, midIPS, PMd, and PMv.
claims.source: When we performed this analysis, we found accurate across-effector classification in four regions during planning: two areas in posterior parietal cortex (PPC), pIPS and midIPS, and two areas in premotor cortex, PMd and PMv (see purple decoding traces and bars in Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results, with reference to a figure.

claims.claim: Accurate across-effector classification cannot be attributed to low-level visual, haptic, or kinematic similarities between hand and tool trials.
claims.source: Importantly, recall that because the object location was changed (with respect to fixation) between hand and tool experimental runs coupled with the fact that the reverse tool required operating mechanics opposite from those required when the hand was used alone, accurate across-effector classification cannot be attributed to low-level visual, haptic, or kinematic similarities between hand and tool trials.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on the experimental design.

claims.claim: Several areas accurately differentiated upcoming movements for both effectors but did not allow for accurate cross-classification.
claims.source: Indeed, although several other areas accurately differentiated the two upcoming movements for both effectors (e.g., post. aIPS, aIPS, t-aIPS, and motor cortex), the preparatory spatial patterns of activity in these areas did not allow for accurate cross-classification.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: In L-SPOC, decoding accuracies for the hand were significantly higher than for the tool and for across-effector decoding.
claims.source: in L-SPOC, decoding accuracies for the hand were significantly higher than for the tool and for across-effector decoding (both at p<0.05; F1.538 = 6.084, p=0.014)
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claims.claim: In L-SMG, decoding accuracies for the tool were significantly higher than for the hand and for across-effector decoding.
claims.source: in L-SMG, decoding accuracies for the tool were significantly higher than for the hand and for across-effector decoding (both at p<0.05; F1.959 = 10.016, p<0.001)
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claims.claim: In L-motor cortex, decoding accuracies for the hand were significantly higher than across-effector decoding.
claims.source: in L-motor cortex, decoding accuracies for the hand were significantly higher than across-effector decoding (p<0.05; F1.398 = 6.239, p=0.016)
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claims.claim: In L-pMTG, decoding accuracies for the tool were significantly higher than for the hand.
claims.source: and lastly, in L-pMTG, decoding accuracies for the tool were significantly higher than for the hand (p=0.049; F1.968 = 4.171, p=0.037)
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claims.claim: Visual inspection of voxel weightings failed to reveal any structured or consistent topography within or across subjects.
claims.source: Visual inspection of the voxel weightings failed to reveal any structured or consistent topography within or across subjects (for similar results, see also Harrison and Tong, 2009; Gallivan et al., 2011a).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the analysis results, with citations to similar findings.

claims.claim: Accurate across-effector classification does not arise in primary auditory cortex during the pre-defined plan-epoch.
claims.source: We found that although accurate across-effector classification does indeed arise in Heschl's gyrus during the trial, it does so distinctly earlier in the Plan-phase compared to that of the frontoparietal areas (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results, with reference to a figure.

claims.claim: The temporal disconnect between cross-decoding in Heschl's gyrus and frontoparietal cortex makes it unlikely that effector-invariant responses in frontoparietal cortex are attributable to auditory commonalities in planning cues.
claims.source: The temporal disconnect between the cross-decoding found in Heschl's gyrus (which emerges in the fourth volume of the Plan-phase) and frontoparietal cortex (which generally emerges in the fifth-sixth volumes of the Plan-phase) makes it unlikely that the effector-invariant nature of the responses revealed in PPC and premotor cortex can be fully attributable to simple auditory commonalities in the planning cues.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: SPOC and EBA discriminated upcoming hand movements only.
claims.source: At the effector-specific level, we found that SPOC and EBA discriminated upcoming hand movements only
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: SMG and pMTG discriminated upcoming tool movements only.
claims.source: whereas SMG and pMTG discriminated upcoming tool movements only.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Anterior parietal (post. aIPS, aIPS, t-aIPS) and motor cortex areas discriminated planned actions for both hand and tool but did not cross-decode between the two effectors.
claims.source: Furthermore, anterior parietal (post. aIPS, aIPS, t-aIPS) and motor cortex areas discriminated planned actions for both the hand and tool, but did not cross-decode between the two effectors.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: In posterior parietal (pIPS and midIPS) and premotor (PMd and PMv) cortex areas, pre-movement patterns predictive of grasp vs reach actions for the hand also predicted grasp vs reach actions with the tool.
claims.source: At the effector-independent level, in posterior parietal (pIPS and midIPS) and premotor (PMd and PMv) cortex areas, we found that the pre-movement patterns predictive of grasp vs reach actions for the hand also predicted grasp vs reach actions with the tool.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Because the tool-effector required very different hand kinematics than when the hand was used alone, brain areas showing cross-decoding encoded the action performed rather than the specific muscle movements needed to achieve it.
claims.source: Notably, because the tool-effector required very different hand kinematics than when the hand was used alone, this suggests that these brain areas encoded the action performed rather than the specific muscle movements needed to achieve it.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results based on the experimental design.

claims.claim: In the majority of regions tested, neural representations remain linked to either the hand or tool.
claims.source: Notably, however, in the majority of regions tested we find that neural representations remain linked to either the hand or tool.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Hierarchical theories of motor control distinguish between various levels of abstraction required for action planning.
claims.source: Hierarchical theories of motor control have existed for more than a century (Jackson, 1889; Sherrington, 1906; Hebb, 1949), distinguishing between the various levels of abstraction required for action planning—for example, at the level of muscles, joints, motor kinematics, and movement goals.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical theories.

claims.claim: EBA has been implicated in coding movements of the hand/arm.
claims.source: Although typically associated with visual-perceptual processing, EBA, like SPOC, has been implicated in coding movements of the hand/arm (Astafiev et al., 2004; Orlov et al., 2010, although see Peelen and Downing, 2005)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The inability to decode tool movement plans from SPOC and EBA suggests that they fail to incorporate tools into the body schema.
claims.source: and the fact that we were unable to decode tool movement plans from these regions suggests that they fail to incorporate tools into the body schema (see also Gallivan et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results, with a citation.

claims.claim: SMG and pMTG are typically activated when human subjects view or pantomime tool-related actions.
claims.source: SMG and pMTG, in contrast, are typically activated when human subjects view (Lewis, 2006; Peeters et al., 2009) or pantomime (Johnson-Frey et al., 2005) tool-related actions
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Damage to SMG and pMTG creates difficulty in pantomiming or performing tool use actions.
claims.source: and damage to these areas creates difficulty in pantomiming or performing tool use actions (Haaland et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Planning-related signals in SMG and pMTG are able to predict real tool actions.
claims.source: That planning-related signals in SMG and pMTG are able to 'predict' real tool actions, as shown here, provides an important extension of these previous findings
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results and their significance.

claims.claim: SMG and pMTG play an important and selective role in generating object-directed tool actions.
claims.source: demonstrating that these areas also play an important and selective role in generating object-directed tool actions.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Motor cortex provides the largest source of descending motor commands to spinal neurons that produce hand kinematics.
claims.source: These features match the known properties of motor cortex; it provides the largest source of descending motor commands to the spinal neurons that produce hand kinematics (Porter and Lemon, 1993)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: Much of motor cortex activity can be accounted for in muscle control terms.
claims.source: and correspondingly, much of its activity can be accounted for in muscle control terms (see Kalaska, 2009; Churchland et al., 2012; Lillicrap and Scott, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: aIPS has been strongly implicated in grasp planning and execution.
claims.source: In parietal cortex, aIPS has been strongly implicated in grasp planning and execution (e.g., Murata et al., 2000; Culham et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: aIPS has been implicated in tool use.
claims.source: Notably, it has also been implicated in tool use (Gallivan et al., 2009; Jacobs et al., 2010)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The anterior IPS is recruited in the planning of tool actions in addition to those of the hand.
claims.source: First, the anterior IPS is recruited in the planning of tool actions in addition to those of the hand, suggestive of an important role in preparing actions with both effectors.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: The representations in anterior IPS for hand and tool actions may differ, perhaps depending on the specifics of the kinematics or object-effector interactions.
claims.source: Second, this pattern of findings on its own does not demonstrate that hand and tool actions rely on the same underlying representations, as previously interpreted (e.g., Rijntjes et al., 1999; Castiello et al., 2000). Rather, as indicated by our cross-classification findings, the representations may differ, perhaps depending on the specifics of the kinematics or object-effector interactions.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results, with citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The posterior IPS appears to serve a variety of high-level visual-motor- and cognitive-related functions.
claims.source: In the human and macaque monkey, the posterior IPS appears to serve a variety of high-level visual-motor- and cognitive-related functions, such as integrating target- and effector-related information for movement (Andersen and Buneo, 2002) and encoding 3D features of objects for hand actions (Sakata et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Effector-independent responses in posterior IPS may emerge due to a common coding of object features more relevant for grasping than reaching.
claims.source: One possibility, in line with this previous work, is that effector-independent responses in these areas emerge due to a common coding of object features that are more relevant for grasping than reaching.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: PMd and PMv are engaged in hand actions in both monkey and human.
claims.source: We also found evidence for these same types of effector-independent representations in premotor areas, PMd and PMv. Each area is engaged in hand actions in both the monkey (Rizzolatti and Luppino, 2001; Raos et al., 2004, 2006) and human (Davare et al., 2006; Gallivan et al., 2011)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: PMd and PMv are implicated in higher-level goal-related processing.
claims.source: and their implication in higher-level goal-related processing (Rizzolatti and Luppino, 2001; Cisek et al., 2003), particularly in the case of tool use with PMv (Umilta et al., 2008), strongly resonates with the findings reported here.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research and is related to the current findings.

claims.claim: Nearly all fMRI studies examining action-centred coding have adopted tasks that require the observation of others' actions.
claims.source: To date, nearly all fMRI studies examining action-centred coding have done so by adopting tasks that require the observation of others' actions (Lewis, 2006; Grafton and Hamilton, 2007; Peeters et al., 2009; Valyear and Culham, 2010)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: Mirror-neurons in monkey inferior parietal and ventral premotor cortex discharge both when the monkey performs a motor act and when the monkey views the same act performed by another individual.
claims.source: This particular line of research has been primarily motivated by the discovery of 'mirror-neurons' in the monkey (Rizzolatti et al., 2001), located in inferior parietal and ventral premotor cortex (Fogassi et al., 2005; Umilta et al., 2008), which discharge both when the monkey performs a motor act and when the monkey views the same act performed by another individual.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: There is a strong coupling between the categorical-selectivity of a brain region as defined through visual-perceptual processing and its specific role in behavior as defined through movement planning.
claims.source: Here we provide compelling evidence for a strong coupling between the categorical-selectivity of a brain region, as defined through visual-perceptual processing, and its specific role in behavior, as defined through movement planning.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental findings.

claims.claim: The preparatory activity in independently localized body-selective EBA and tool-selective pMTG decoded movement plans for hand and tool actions, respectively.
claims.source: For instance, in occipitotemporal cortex we found that the preparatory activity in the independently localized body-selective EBA and the tool-selective pMTG decoded movement plans for hand and tool actions, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Hand- and tool-related actions at certain cortical processing levels may recruit distinct neural populations, similar to the highly modular nature of visual-perceptual processing in occipitotemporal cortex.
claims.source: This indicates that, similar to the highly modular nature of visual-perceptual processing in occipitotemporal cortex (Downing et al., 2006; Kanwisher, 2010), hand- and tool-related actions at certain cortical processing levels may also recruit distinct neural populations.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results, with citations.

claims.claim: Upcoming movements for both hand and tool could be decoded from the independently defined tool-selective t-aIPS.
claims.source: As an interesting departure from these occipitotemporal cortex results, we found that we could decode upcoming movements for 'both' the hand and tool from the independently defined tool-selective t-aIPS.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: The decoding of tool actions in t-aIPS is congruent with its activation in observation-based tool-related tasks.
claims.source: At the functional level, the decoding of tool actions in t-aIPS is entirely congruent with its activation in observation-based tool-related tasks (for reviews, see Lewis, 2006; Frey, 2007)
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in the context of previous research.

claims.claim: The decoding of hand actions in t-aIPS accords with its close proximity to parietal areas involved in hand preshaping and manipulation.
claims.source: and, at the anatomical level, the decoding of hand actions in t-aIPS accords with its close proximity to parietal areas involved in hand preshaping and manipulation (Culham et al., 2003; Valyear et al., 2007; Gallivan et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in the context of previous research.

claims.claim: Hand and tool movement planning may only begin recruiting similar neural structures at the level of parietal cortex.
claims.source: When compared to the findings in occipitotemporal cortex, this result indicates that hand and tool movement planning may only begin recruiting similar neural structures at the level of parietal cortex.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: The signals in EBA and pMTG reflect the intention to perform a motor act rather than the sensory feedback responses that accompany it.
claims.source: Although others have shown that hand/arm movements can activate different regions in occipitotemporal cortex (Astafiev et al., 2004; Filimon et al., 2009; Cavina-Pratesi et al., 2010; Oosterhof et al., 2010; Orlov et al., 2010), here we demonstrate that these signals reflect the 'intention' to perform a motor act rather than the sensory feedback responses (visual, proprioceptive, tactile) that accompany it.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in the context of previous research.

claims.claim: EBA and pMTG may play a significant role in action planning and control by predicting the sensory consequences of actions/movement before those consequences unfold.
claims.source: This distinction is important because it indicates that these occipitotemporal cortex areas may play a significant role in action planning and control, possibly by predicting the sensory consequences of actions/movement even before those consequences unfold.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Forward-state estimations at the level of occipitotemporal cortex remain linked to the type of effector to be used in an upcoming movement.
claims.source: The current findings would suggest that such forward-state estimations, at least at the level of occipitotemporal cortex, remain linked to the type of effector (hand vs tool) to be used in an upcoming movement.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Hand- and tool-related action plans can be decoded from preparatory signals in body- and tool-selective occipitotemporal cortex areas.
claims.source: Updating the considerably simpler notion that action planning, particularly in the case of tool use, merely involves 'access' to ventral stream resources (Milner and Goodale, 1995; Valyear and Culham, 2010), these findings show that hand- and tool-related action plans can actually be decoded from preparatory signals in body- and tool-selective occipitotemporal cortex areas.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental findings in the context of previous theories.

claims.claim: The organization of occipitotemporal cortex may emerge as a by-product of the distinct connectivity patterns of OTC areas with downstream motor structures.
claims.source: One particularly compelling alternative view, however, argues that the organization of OTC may be largely invariant to bottom-up visual properties and that it instead emerges as a by-product of the distinct connectivity patterns of OTC areas with the rest of the brain, particularly the downstream motor structures that use the visual information processed in OTC to plan movements of the body (Mahon et al., 2007; Mahon and Caramazza, 2009, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous theoretical work.

claims.claim: The neural specificity for visual presentation of body parts and/or tools in OTC may reflect anatomical connectivity with frontoparietal areas involved in generating movements of the body and/or interacting with tools.
claims.source: Under this view, the neural specificity frequently observed for the visual presentation of body parts and/or tools in particular regions of OTC may reflect, to a certain extent, their anatomical connectivity with frontoparietal areas involved in generating movements of the body and/or interacting with and manipulating tools, respectively—a notion that garners some empirical support from the 'downstream' functional connectivity patterns of areas involved in body part- and tool-related processing (Mahon et al., 2007; Bracci et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The visual-response selectivity of neurons in AIP for size, shape, orientation, etc. are often matched to their motor-response selectivity during action.
claims.source: This compatibility of visual- and motor-related responses within single brain areas resonates with neurophysiological findings in macaque parietal cortex showing that the visual-response selectivity of neurons in AIP (for size, shape, orientation, etc.) are often matched to their motor-response selectivity during action (e.g., Murata et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous neurophysiological research.

claims.claim: The coupling of visual and motor selectivity is thought to mediate the transformation of visual information regarding physical object properties into corresponding motor programs for grasping or use.
claims.source: This coupling is thought to mediate the transformation of visual information regarding physical object properties into corresponding motor programs for grasping or use (Jeannerod et al., 1995; Rizzolatti and Luppino, 2001)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The specificity of visual object categorical responses in OTC are in some way linked to a specific role in preparing related motor behaviors.
claims.source: Where exactly the current findings fit within the context of these broader frameworks remains unclear, nevertheless, our results provide novel evidence suggesting that the specificity of visual object categorical responses in OTC are in some way linked to a specific role in preparing related motor behaviors.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results in the context of broader theoretical frameworks.

claims.claim: Eight of the thirteen participants from the Motor experiment participated in a second Localizer experiment.
claims.source: A subset of participants from the motor experiment (n = 8) were recruited for a second localizer experiment.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods.

claims.claim: The purpose of the Localizer experiment was to localize visual-perceptual ROIs involved in body- and tool-selective processing.
claims.source: The purpose of this second scan session was to localize well-documented visual-perceptual ROIs involved in body- and tool-selective processing and then examine, using the motor experiment data from these same subjects, whether hand and tool movement plans could be decoded from these separately identified object-selective areas.
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods.

claims.claim: EBA has been widely implicated in coding perceptual functions related to the body.
claims.source: One area of interest, EBA, has been widely implicated in coding perceptual functions related to the body, including the identification of other individuals, the processing of others' emotional states and movements, as well as perception of the self and representations of the body schema (Downing and Peelen, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claims.claim: pMTG has been implicated in coding numerous perceptual functions related to tools.
claims.source: Likewise, pMTG has been implicated in coding numerous perceptual functions related to tools, including tool motion, identification, naming, auditory processing, and the retrieval of semantic information concerning their use (e.g., Martin et al., 1996; Beauchamp and Martin, 2007; Lewis et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: EBA and pMTG are activated by self-generated movements.
claims.source: Interestingly, both ROIs are also activated by self-generated movements (unseen hand actions in the case of EBA and pantomimed tool actions in the case of pMTG; Lewis, 2006; Frey, 2007; Downing and Peelen, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: The localizer task used static color photos of familiar tools, headless bodies, non-tool objects, and scrambled versions of these stimuli.
claims.source: To localize these visual-perceptual ROIs we used a standard block-design localizer task in which participants were required to view static color photos of familiar tools, headless bodies, non-tool objects, and scrambled up versions of these same stimuli (Figure 5A for timing and protocol; see also Valyear and Culham, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental methods, with reference to a figure.

claims.claim: pMTG and t-aIPS were identified as tool-specific activations using a conjunction contrast.
claims.source: To identify the brain areas selectively involved in tool-related visual processing, in each subject we searched for regions showing heightened activation for tools compared to headless bodies, non-tool objects, and scrambled stimuli (conjunction contrast: [(Tools > Bodies) AND (Tools > Objects) AND (Tools > Scrambled)], t = 3, p<0.005, corrected). Across subjects, this contrast revealed consistent activity in two brain regions: 1) pMTG and 2) an area located anteriorly along the IPS (tool-aIPS, t-aIPS).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: EBA was identified as a body-selective region using a conjunction contrast.
claims.source: We next searched for body-selective regions by contrasting activity for bodies compared to tools, non-tool objects, and scrambled stimuli (conjunction contrast: [(Bodies > Tools) AND (Bodies > Objects) AND (Bodies > Scrambled)], t = 3, p<0.005, corrected). Across subjects, this contrast revealed consistent activity in EBA
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: pMTG was characteristically positioned lateral, ventral, and anterior to EBA in each subject.
claims.source: Notably, in each subject we found a highly consistent spatial relationship between EBA and pMTG: pMTG was characteristically positioned lateral, ventral, and anterior to EBA (consistent with Valyear and Culham, 2010).
claims.evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental results, with a citation.

claims.claim: Predictive movement information generally arises in the two time points prior to initiation of the movement.
claims.source: First, predictive movement information, if it is to emerge, generally arises in the two time points prior to initiation of the movement (although note that in a few brain areas, such as L-pIPS and L-PMd, this information is also available prior to these two time points).
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental results.

claims.claim: Accurate classification never arises prior to the subject being aware of which action to execute.
claims.source: Second, in support of the notion that this predictive motor information is directly related to the 'intention' to make a movement, accurate classification never arises prior to the subject being aware of which action to execute (i.e., prior to the auditory instruction delivered at the initiation of the Plan phase).
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental results and their interpretation.

claims.claim: Decoding related to movement planning can be fully disentangled from decoding related to movement execution.
claims.source: Finally, decoding related to the planning of a movement can be fully disentangled from decoding related to movement execution, which generally arises several imaging volumes later.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement of the experimental results.

results.result: The study used fMRI with MVPA to decode hand and tool movement plans in 13 subjects performing grasp and reach actions with either their hand or reverse tongs. The experimental design included a delayed-movement paradigm that isolated planning-related neural responses from visual and execution responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C25, C31, C93-C94 describe the experimental design and methods. The methodology is clearly described with appropriate controls (reverse tongs requiring opposite kinematics, delayed paradigm, position changes between effectors). The design allows for isolation of planning signals and testing of effector-specific vs effector-independent representations.

results.result: Tool use is subserved by multiple distributed neural representations that are both shared with and distinct from hand representations. SPOC and EBA showed hand-specific coding, SMG and pMTG showed tool-specific coding, anterior parietal regions and motor cortex showed separate coding for both effectors, while posterior IPS and premotor cortex showed effector-independent coding.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3, C26-C30, C40, C52-C55 present the core findings supported by MVPA decoding results. The experimental design with reverse tongs and position changes rules out low-level confounds (C41). Statistical tests confirm significant differences in decoding patterns across regions (C45-C48). The hierarchical organization is well-supported by converging evidence across multiple ROIs.

results.result: Time-resolved decoding revealed that preparatory movement information arises in the two time points prior to movement initiation, never before subjects are aware of which action to execute, and can be fully disentangled from execution-related activity. Nearly all frontoparietal regions could decode planned actions for both hand and tool effectors.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C39, C102-C104 describe temporal dynamics of decoding. The time-resolved analysis shows appropriate temporal separation between planning and execution phases. The sensory control region (SS-cortex) behaves as expected (C39), validating the approach. The findings are consistent with the delayed paradigm design.

results.result: Accurate across-effector classification cannot be attributed to low-level similarities between hand and tool trials because the reverse tool required opposite kinematics and object position changed between runs. Brain areas showing cross-decoding encoded the action performed rather than specific muscle movements.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42, C56 address critical interpretational issues. The experimental design explicitly controls for kinematic and visual confounds through use of reverse tongs and position changes. The logic is sound: if cross-decoding succeeds despite these differences, it must reflect higher-level action goals rather than low-level features.

results.result: Statistical analyses revealed significant differences in decoding accuracies across regions: SPOC showed higher hand than tool decoding, SMG showed higher tool than hand decoding, motor cortex showed higher hand than across-effector decoding, and pMTG showed higher tool than hand decoding.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C48 report specific statistical comparisons with p-values and F-statistics. The statistical tests are appropriate (repeated-measures ANOVA with follow-up t-tests). However, the omnibus test showed only a trend (p=0.069), and only a few specific comparisons reached significance after correction. The pattern is consistent but statistical power appears limited.

results.result: Visual inspection of voxel weightings failed to reveal structured or consistent topography within or across subjects.
results.evaluation: Claim C49 reports a null finding regarding voxel weight topography. The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation and provide reasonable explanations (relatively low decoding accuracies, trial-to-trial variability). They cite similar findings in other studies, suggesting this is a known characteristic of MVPA with planning signals.

results.result: Accurate across-effector classification in primary auditory cortex (Heschl's gyrus) arises earlier in the Plan phase than in frontoparietal areas, making it unlikely that effector-invariant responses in frontoparietal cortex are attributable to auditory commonalities in planning cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C51 address an important alternative explanation. The temporal dissociation between auditory cortex cross-decoding (4th volume) and frontoparietal cross-decoding (5th-6th volumes) provides evidence against a simple auditory confound. This control analysis strengthens the interpretation of frontoparietal findings.

results.result: Hand- and tool-related actions are represented separately at earlier levels of sensorimotor processing before becoming integrated in frontoparietal cortex. The hierarchical organization suggests that in the majority of regions, neural representations remain linked to either hand or tool, with only posterior IPS and premotor cortex showing effector-independent coding.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C30, C57, C60, C64, C69-C70, C83 present interpretations of the hierarchical organization. These interpretations are well-supported by the pattern of results across regions. The claim that representations are 'separate at earlier levels' is consistent with the occipitotemporal findings (SPOC, EBA, SMG, pMTG) and anterior parietal findings (aIPS, motor cortex).

results.result: There is strong coupling between the categorical-selectivity of brain regions defined through visual-perceptual processing and their specific role in movement planning. Preparatory activity in body-selective EBA and tool-selective pMTG decoded movement plans for hand and tool actions respectively, indicating that hand- and tool-related action plans can be decoded from body- and tool-selective occipitotemporal cortex areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C79, C87, C92 describe the coupling between perceptual selectivity and motor planning. The localizer experiment independently identified EBA and pMTG based on visual selectivity, and the motor experiment showed corresponding motor selectivity. This provides strong evidence for the coupling, though the sample size for the localizer experiment was smaller (n=8).

results.result: Upcoming movements for both hand and tool could be decoded from the independently defined tool-selective t-aIPS. This decoding is congruent with t-aIPS activation in observation-based tool tasks and its proximity to parietal areas involved in hand preshaping.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 describe t-aIPS findings. The region shows both hand and tool decoding despite being defined as tool-selective in the localizer. This is interpreted as reflecting the transition from effector-specific to effector-independent coding at the level of parietal cortex. The interpretation is reasonable given the anatomical location and functional properties.

results.result: The signals in EBA and pMTG reflect the intention to perform a motor act rather than sensory feedback responses. These occipitotemporal cortex areas may play a significant role in action planning by predicting sensory consequences of actions before they unfold, with forward-state estimations remaining linked to the type of effector.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 present interpretations about the nature of signals in EBA and pMTG. While the delayed paradigm does isolate planning from execution, the claim that these signals represent 'forward-state estimations' is speculative (C85 is marked as SPECULATION). The interpretation is plausible but goes beyond what the data directly demonstrate.

results.result: The findings fit within hierarchical theories of motor control, with different brain regions situated at different levels of abstraction. SPOC and EBA code hand movements, SMG and pMTG code tool movements, anterior parietal regions and motor cortex code effector-specific kinematics, and posterior IPS and premotor cortex code higher-level action goals.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C74 integrate the findings with prior knowledge and theoretical frameworks. The interpretations are well-grounded in the data and appropriately cite relevant literature. The hierarchical interpretation is consistent with the pattern of results and with established theories of motor control.

results.result: The organization of occipitotemporal cortex may emerge as a by-product of distinct connectivity patterns with downstream motor structures. The neural specificity for visual presentation of body parts and tools in OTC may reflect anatomical connectivity with frontoparietal areas involved in generating movements of the body and interacting with tools.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C91 present theoretical interpretations about the organization of OTC. These are based on citations to previous theoretical work (C88-C89) and neurophysiological findings (C90-C91). While the current findings are consistent with these theories, the study does not directly test connectivity or provide new evidence for these organizational principles.

results.result: Tool use involves transfer of proximal hand goals to distal tool goals. Previous research in macaque monkeys showed that neurons encoding hand grasping subsequently encoded tool grasping, suggesting effector-independent representation. Tools may become incorporated into the body schema following training.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10 summarize prior work that motivated the current study. These are appropriately cited and provide important context. However, these are not results of the current study but rather background claims from the literature.

results.result: Previous fMRI research has identified specialized regions in frontoparietal and occipitotemporal cortex that selectively represent tools and bodies. SMG, pMTG, and PMd show evolutionary expansion in humans and are co-activated during tool use tasks. However, almost all prior neuroimaging studies used proxies for real tool use rather than actual tool actions.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C19, C32-C33, C75-C76 provide background on prior research. These are well-cited and accurately represent the literature. The claim about proxies for tool use (C19) is important for establishing the novelty of the current study. These are not results of the current study but provide essential context.

results.result: The localizer experiment used static color photos to identify body-selective EBA and tool-selective pMTG and t-aIPS. EBA and pMTG have been implicated in perceptual functions related to bodies and tools respectively, and are also activated by self-generated movements. pMTG was consistently positioned lateral, ventral, and anterior to EBA.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C101 describe the localizer experiment methods and results. The methods are standard and well-described. The localizer successfully identified the target ROIs in individual subjects. The spatial relationship between EBA and pMTG (C101) is consistent with previous work. However, only 8 of 13 subjects participated in the localizer experiment.

results.result: Sophisticated tool use is a defining characteristic of the primate species.
results.evaluation: Claim C1 is a general statement about primate characteristics based on established knowledge. While accurate, this is background information rather than a result of the current study.

results.result: SS-cortex was selected as a sensory control region not expected to accurately decode movements until stimulation of the hand's mechanoreceptors at movement onset.
results.evaluation: Claim C34 describes the rationale for including SS-cortex as a control. This is appropriate experimental design. The expectation was confirmed by the results (C39), validating the approach.
